text: Two minutes past eight, on a Monday morning.
A man swings a sledgehammer at a window.
It bounces.
Another man charges it with a battering ram. Seventy kilos.
Nothing.
The man who planned this had said the glass would break like a cracker.
He had given it fifteen seconds.
Stavanger. Norway's oil city.
Behind the old cathedral square, below street level, was a room where the region's cash was counted.
In two thousand and four, the company that ran it, NOKAS, was about to move somewhere far more secure.
For one man, that meant now, or never.
His name was David Toska.
In two thousand and three, he moved to Sandnes, just south of the city, with his partner and their newborn son.
As a teenager, he had been a talented chess player.
He thought in moves.
And every board needs a way in.
The way in came from a young security guard. Twenty-six years old.
He met Toska several times. He described the courtyard. He drew the rooms.
And he talked about a window. The glass into the basement.
He says he thought it was a burglary. He got three years.
From a small atrium in that courtyard, you could see straight into the counting room.
One of the robbers later described it.
You see the vaults being opened at eight. You see pallets of money, and you know there are hundreds of millions there.
Between him and the money, there was one pane of glass.
Monday, the second of February. Toska lay in that courtyard, freezing, waiting.
And the robbery was called off.
Why depends on who you ask. One account says he saw the money being moved out. Another says the radios failed.
Four days later, everything changed.
On the sixth of February, in Oslo, Toska's best friend was shot dead.
His name was William Ellingsen. He was twenty-nine. And he had helped plan the robbery.
A stray bullet, through a door. He was not the target.
At the funeral, Toska gave the eulogy.
Afterwards, the plan changed.
It had to be spectacular, he decided. Massive. More men.
One of them later said William's death led to irrational planning.
He wanted the robbery to be a monument to his friend.
It would become a monument.
Just not to William.
They rehearsed the escape, on footpaths and unfinished cycle paths.
They gathered mattresses, bedding and towels, to soak in fuel and burn inside a truck.
Fire would take care of the evidence.
Monday, the fifteenth of March. A second attempt. A red alarm light. A guard.
Called off again.
They chose a third date. Monday, the fifth of April. Easter week. Many police officers on holiday.
But the police had heard something.
Warnings. A working group. A thirteen-page intelligence document.
On Friday, the second of April, revolvers went into three patrol cars instead of two.
The warning did not reach everyone it should have. An official inquiry later called it a system failure.
One of the men who did read it was Arne Sigve Klungland.
Fifty-three. Thirty years in the police. Dog handler. Rescue leader. He trained police students.
And on church trips, he was the one who drove the pensioners' bus.
Half past three in the morning. A van collected them from Toska's townhouse and drove them to the woods.
Before they left, they taped white bands onto their overalls.
Mourning bands. For William.
No battle cry. Just silence.
That morning, at the police briefing, it was Klungland who passed the warning on to the patrols.
One of the officers, Erik Håland, said later: "That's when I understood this was serious."
Two rooms, getting ready for the same morning.
Seven-forty. Security cameras show eleven men, dressed and armed.
Eight o'clock. A white truck is driven into the police station's driveway and set alight. Tear gas at the entrance.
Two minutes, fifty-eight seconds past eight. The police register the alarm.
Toska fired at the glass himself.
Then he fetched Schumann, who emptied magazine after magazine along the edge of the window.
One hundred and thirteen shots.
Below them, three women who worked there pushed two trolleys into the lift.
On the trolleys: sixty million kroner.
As the doors closed, they could hear the gunfire.
Upstairs, the window finally gave way. They were in.
It was eight minutes past eight. Six minutes behind the plan.
And outside, the first police car had just turned onto the cathedral square.
They had brought fifteen bags, for three or four hundred million kroner.
What they found was mostly blue two-hundred-kroner notes.
There was a barred gate to the main vault. They hit it with the ram. It didn't move.
Toska ran from room to room with a watch in his hand.
The plan said eight minutes. It was going to take nearly twenty.
Outside, two officers, Erik Håland and Steffen Thesen, had revolvers. Twelve rounds each.
Against them, military rifles.
At a street corner, Schumann forced a plain-clothes officer to the ground. "Who are you?"
And all around them, the city kept going. A bus. People on their way to work. Women pushing prams.
Some thought it was an exercise.
Fourteen minutes past eight. Shooting across the square. One of the robbers was hit in the leg.
More police came. Among them, the command vehicle. In it, Arne Sigve Klungland, driving toward the shooting.
Seventeen minutes past eight.
He tried to reverse.
There was a bus behind him.
Arne Sigve Klungland was killed there. He was fifty-three.
At twenty past eight, the last car left the square, still firing.
In the woods at Sørmarka, they set the cars on fire and drove on in others.
The fire was supposed to erase them. It didn't.
The truck barely burned, and the fire station was right next door.
Later that day, six of them sat in a flat on Nedre Dalgate, a few hundred metres from the square, with the money.
On the television, they learned that a police officer was dead.
On the fourteenth of April, about six hundred police officers came to Stavanger Cathedral.
A helicopter flew low over the city.
Arne Sigve Klungland had been married since nineteen seventy-seven. He left a wife and two children.
In the counting room, the police found an earplug. Toska had lost it. Inside was his DNA.
And the barred gate to the main vault, the one they had battered and could not break,
had never been locked.
They could have reached in and lifted the handle.
Downstairs, three women had saved sixty million. More than the robbers took.
Toska ran. To a village in southern Spain, with his partner and their baby.
In Oslo, a police data specialist they called the Sharp Knife watched the internet cafés.
They found his email address: omaha beach, at postmaster.
In Madrid, Spanish police reached a café five minutes too late.
One reporter later called it a chess game. The Sharp Knife, against the man the press called the Mastermind.
The fifth of April, two thousand and five. One year to the day.
At the request of the Norwegian police, his email provider slowed logins across Europe.
Toska stayed online longer than usual, reading news from home, about the memorial for Arne Sigve Klungland.
In Stavanger, that memorial was under way.
In Málaga, police walked into the café.
In Stavanger, the news went through the gathering like a murmur.
Thirteen men were convicted.
Schumann admitted firing the shots that killed Klungland. He says it was a mistake. The court found it was an aimed shot.
Toska was sentenced to eighteen years.
About fifty-one million kroner has never been found.
Ten years later, thirty-two people who worked at NOKAS still carried that morning with them.
He had planned for the glass. The police. The city.
But the one thing that could never be replaced…
was never on his board.
